case.presentation: A 27-year-old man with no history of allergies presents with truncal-predominant, pruritic hives for 6 weeks. It is unrelated to hot showers and without other symptoms. He has used near-daily cetirizine for 2 weeks and diphenhydramine when intense; no new detergents/body washes. Suspected chronic urticaria (raised, pruritic welts that resolve within 24 hours; may be spontaneous or inducible). What prophylactic regimen and counseling are recommended, which cofactors to avoid, when to refer for possible urticarial vasculitis, and how to escalate therapy if not controlled?
case.recommendations: Increase cetirizine 10 mg to BID for prophylaxis, counseling on risks including sedation and/or dry mouth. Continue antihistamine prophylaxis until complete control, then attempt to wean. Advise against first-generation antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine) due to sedation and other side effects. Advise patient to maintain a symptom diary noting any new medications or exposures. Avoid cofactors that exacerbate urticaria: hot showers, tight clothing, NSAIDs/ASA, opiates, stress, alcohol. This is not angioedema, so ACE-I do not need to be avoided. Take additional history to identify any exacerbating factors such as new medications. Would also consider screening labs for chronic urticaria assessment (CBC with differential, ESR, CRP) if appropriate. Refer to Allergy if red flags for urticarial vasculitis: hives persisting >24 hours, residual bruising/scarring, or painful lesions; patient should seek evaluation promptly if they occur. If uncontrolled, increase up to cetirizine 20 mg BID and refer to Allergy for potential escalation (e.g., omalizumab).
